title: You can be Moses (Teshuvah 5:2)
hook: every person can become righteous like Moses or wicked like Jeroboam

segments.voice: Yesterday, the path of return: recognize, regret, confess, resolve. Today, the question underneath it: can a person really change?

Two names sit side by side in a law book. One is Moses, who stood on the mountain and brought down the Torah. The other is Jeroboam, a king of Israel who set up golden calves and led people away. You might expect a writer to put them at opposite ends of the universe, made of different stuff. Maimonides does something stranger. In the middle of his laws of return, he puts the two names in the same sentence, and he puts you between them. Either one, he says, is open to you.
screen: `MOSES ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `JEROBOAM AND THE CALVES.` → `AND YOU, BETWEEN THEM.`

segments.voice: You can be Moses. It's from the fifth chapter of the Laws of Repentance in the Mishneh Torah. First, the claim. Permission is given to every human being, Maimonides writes. Want to turn toward the good way and be righteous? You can. Toward the bad way? You can. Every person can be righteous like Moses our teacher, or wicked like Jeroboam. Wise or foolish, merciful or cruel. Second, what he's pushing against. He calls foolish the idea that God decrees at birth whether a person will be righteous or wicked. Nobody forces a person, nobody decrees it, nobody drags them down either road. The person chooses. Third, why it sits here. If your character were fixed at birth, regret would be pointless and resolve would be theater. Return only works if the road can change direction. He calls this freedom a great principle, a pillar of the Torah and the commandments, and grounds it in Deuteronomy, where life and good, death and evil, are set before the people, and the call comes: "therefore choose life." Fourth, the hard part. If God knows everything ahead of time, how can a person really choose? He doesn't wave it away. The answer is beyond human understanding, he says, because God's knowing is not like ours, and he holds on to both. God knows, and you choose. Readers have argued about that answer. But the sentence about Moses stands either way. Nothing written at your birth closes the road.
screen: `EVERY PERSON CAN TURN EITHER WAY.` · `NOTHING DECREED AT BIRTH.` · `WITHOUT CHOICE, NO RETURN.` · `GOD KNOWS, AND YOU CHOOSE.` · then, large: `YOU CAN BE MOSES.`

segments.voice: Notice the small choices already in this moment: whether to keep sitting, whether to follow a thought or let it go, whether to breathe a little slower. Then think of one moment in your day where you usually run on autopilot, the reply you always give, the scroll you always start, and decide freely what you'd do there instead. If you pray, you can hold the words "therefore choose life" for a breath.
You can be Moses. Maimonides' teaching that every person is free to become righteous like Moses or wicked like Jeroboam, and nothing at birth decides it. Today's word.
Your line: you can be moses. Either road is open, and the choosing is yours. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Jews study the Mishneh Torah's Laws of Repentance, including chapter five on free choice, in the season before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, when return is the theme.

notes: Hilchot Teshuvah 5:1–2 paraphrased: permission given to every person; righteous like Moses or wicked like Jeroboam, wise or foolish, merciful or cruel; the 'fools' who say God decrees at birth. Please confirm.

5:3 calls free choice a great principle and pillar of Torah and commandments, citing Deuteronomy 30:15 ('see, I have set before thee'); the script quotes 30:19 'therefore choose life' instead as the familiar verse. Confirm this pairing is acceptable, and confirm the JPS 1917 wording.
5:5 (God's knowledge and human choice; beyond human understanding) summarized. 'Readers have argued about that answer ever since' alludes to the Raavad's gloss and later discussion; kept general.
Original: רְשׁוּת as Maimonides' word in 5:1 ('רשות לכל אדם נתונה'); please confirm vocalization and gloss.
Jeroboam described from 1 Kings 12 (golden calves); confirm.
